meta.content: A tutorial for adding a command line interface to a Hydra program.
meta.name: description

admonition.title: Prerequisites
admonition.paragraph: This tutorial assumes that you have completed the earlier tutorial: Create and Launch a Basic Application with Hydra

section.names: add\ a\ command\ line\ interface\ to\ our\ application cli-app
section.title: Add a Command Line Interface to Our Application
section.paragraph: In this tutorial we will update our project so that it can be configured and launched from a command line interface (CLI), using Hydra.
In the last section of the tutorial, we

list_item.paragraph: Created a config for that task function
Ran the task function via hydra_zen.launch(Config, task_function, overrides=<...>)

section.paragraph: In this section, we need to add our config to Hydra’s config-store; this enables Hydra to generate a CLI from this config.

section.title: Modifying Our Project
section.paragraph: Open my_app.py in your editor. We will make the following modifications to it:

list_item.paragraph: Use hydra_zen.ZenStore to store our config locally.
Add a __main__ clause to our my_app.py script so that the script runs our task function.
Within __main__ populate Hydra’s global config store so that Hydra can generate a CLI using our configs.
Use hydra_zen.zen() to wrap the task function and to generate the CLI.

section.paragraph: Modify your script to match this:

container.caption: Contents of my_app.py:
container.literal_block:
from hydra_zen import builds, zen, ZenStore
# The same task function as before def task_function(player1: str, player2: str): with open("player_log.txt", "w") as f: f.write("Game session log:\n") f.write(f"Player 1: {player1}\n" f"Player 2: {player2}")
return player1, player2
Config = builds(task_function, populate_full_signature=True)
# 1) Create a local config store and store our config store = ZenStore() store(Config, name="my_app")
# 2) Adding our __main__ clause to our script. # Executing `python my_app.py [...]` will generate a CLI for our running # our task function if __name__ == "__main__": # 3) We need to add the configs from our local store to Hydra's # global config store store.add_to_hydra_store()
# 4) hydra_main generates a CLI based off of the config # stored under the name "my_app", and will run # `task_function` zen(task_function).hydra_main(config_name="my_app", version_base="1.1", config_path=None, )

section.names: launching\ our\ application\ from\ the\ command\ line
section.title: Launching Our Application from the Command Line
section.paragraph: With the above modifications to my_app.py complete, we can launch our application from the command line. The following will launch a job with mario and luigi as the names for player 1 and player 2, respectively.
Open your terminal in the same directory as my_app.py. We can view the configurable aspects of our application using the --help command; run the following:

container.caption: Checking the configurable components of our app. (We will add configuration groups in a later lesson.)
container.literal_block:
$ python my_app.py --help my_app is powered by Hydra.
== Configuration groups == Compose your configuration from those groups (group=option)
== Config == Override anything in the config (foo.bar=value)
player1: ??? player2: ???

section.paragraph: See that our app requires that we configure two fields: player1 and player2. Let’s configure these fields with the string values "mario" and "luigi", respectively. In your console execute the following command:

container.caption: Launching our application from the command line

tip.paragraph: You can add tab-completion to your application’s command line interface. This is helpful once you start writing applications that have many configurable components.

section.paragraph: To inspect the log written by our application, open a Python terminal in the same directory as my_app.py and define the following function for reading files
section.literal_block: >>> from pathlib import Path >>> def print_file(x: Path): ... with x.open("r") as f: ... print(f.read())
section.paragraph: Getting the directory containing the output of this job:
section.literal_block: >>> *_, latest_job = sorted((Path.cwd() / "outputs").glob("*/*")) >>> latest_job # changes based on reader's date, time, and OS WindowsPath('C:/outputs/2021-10-21/12-58-13')
section.paragraph: Print the contents of player_log.txt and verify that it matches with how we ran our program:
section.literal_block: >>> print_file(latest_job / "player_log.txt") Game session log: Player 1: mario Player 2: luigi
section.paragraph: Voilà! As demonstrated, our simple application can now be configured and launched from the command line. It should be noted that we can still launch our app from a Python console, using launch(), as we did in the previous tutorial.
